title: Parents and family
hookLine: worship Allah, then be good to parents, repeated across the book (17:23; 31:14)

cards: Take a highlighter to the Qur'an and mark the places where it says worship Allah alone. Then look at what sits right next to the highlight.
In al-Baqarah, an-Nisa, al-An'am and al-Isra, the very next thing is the same: and be good to your parents. Not your nation, not your teacher, not even your own soul.
In those verses, the command right after the oneness of God is about two people at a kitchen table.

teach.b: Surah al-Isra, verse twenty-three: your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents. Then it gets specific.
If one or both reach old age with you, don't say even uff to them, don't push them away, and speak to them with honor.
Surah Luqman, verse fourteen, gives the reason, and it's the mother's: she carried him, weakness upon weakness, and his weaning took two years. Then: be grateful to Me and to your parents.
Gratitude to Allah and to parents, in one breath. A hadith in al-Bukhari sharpens it. A man asks the Prophet ﷺ: who most deserves my good company?
Your mother. Then who? Your mother.
Then who? Your mother. Then who?
Your father. And the book is honest that family can be hard.

The next verse in Luqman says that if parents push you to worship other than Allah, don't obey them in that, but still keep company with them in this world, kindly. Disagreement doesn't cancel kindness.
Then the circle widens. Remember rahim, the womb, from five days ago, sharing a root with ar-Rahman?
Keeping family ties is called silat ar-rahim, connecting the womb. A hadith in al-Bukhari says the rahim takes its name from ar-Rahman, and whoever keeps it connected, Allah keeps connected to them.
Family, in this vocabulary, is mercy's own shape.

how: Muslims treat kindness to parents (birr al-walidayn) as a duty that comes right after worshipping Allah, and keeping family ties (silat ar-rahim) as a religious obligation; the Qur'an's own prayer for parents (17:24) is said in personal du'a.

o: a word for the eldest son of a family
a word for a parent's strict authority
the womb, from the same root as mercy

games.q: parents and family — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an mentions kindness to parents only once
it pairs it with worshipping Allah again and again: 2:83, 4:36, 6:151, 17:23.
the Qur'an says to stay kind to parents even when you disagree on faith
31:15: don't obey them in that, but keep company with them kindly.
rahim, the womb, shares a root with ar-Rahman
a hadith says the rahim takes its name from ar-Rahman.

games.q: a man asks the Prophet: who most deserves my good company? what is the answer, in order?
o: your mother, your mother, your mother, then your father.
games.why: your mother, three times, then your father (Sahih al-Bukhari 5971).

practice: Bring your family to mind, the one you were born into or the one you've found, and let a parent's face come, or a grandparent's, or whoever raised you.

If they've died and you pray, ask mercy for them; if they're alive, picture them right now, doing something ordinary, and choose one kindness for them: a call, a visit, an errand, a word of thanks, or simply not saying uff.

wordCard.voice: Rahim: the womb, sharing its root with ar-Rahman, the word underneath the command to keep family ties connected. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: parents come next. Right after Allah, two people at a kitchen table. Until tomorrow.
